subject: Accounting
title: The SEC and Financial Regulation
description: A 60-second lesson on The SEC and Financial Regulation.

hook.text: The SEC has the power to shut down companies that lie about their numbers.

buildup.text: Created in 1934, it oversees financial reporting for all U.S. publicly traded companies.

discovery.text: The SEC delegated standard-setting to private bodies—first the APB, now the FASB.

twist.text: The SEC rarely writes rules itself, but its enforcement power gives those rules teeth.

climax.text: Without the SEC, accounting standards would be suggestions. With it, they're law.

punchline.text: Rules without enforcement are just suggestions.

quiz.question: Who currently sets U.S. accounting standards?

details.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission was created in 1934 to regulate financial markets and enforce honest financial reporting, establishing the government oversight framework that protects investors and maintains market integrity.
details.whyItMatters: The SEC's creation established that truthful financial reporting is not optional but legally required, transforming accounting from a business convenience into a matter of securities law.
takeaways: The SEC was created in 1934 in response to the stock market crash and Great Depression
It has authority to set financial reporting requirements for all publicly traded companies
The SEC enforces accounting rules through investigations, fines, and criminal referrals

faq.question: What does the SEC do for accounting?
faq.answer: The SEC requires all publicly traded companies to file standardized financial statements, sets disclosure requirements, and enforces compliance through investigations and penalties. It delegates detailed accounting rule-making to FASB but retains ultimate authority.

faq.question: Why was the SEC created?
faq.answer: The SEC was created in 1934 after the 1929 stock market crash exposed widespread financial fraud and misleading corporate accounting. Congress established the SEC to restore investor confidence by requiring truthful, standardized financial disclosures.
